narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 21, it is far below the average of 37 among students who were admitted, signaling that the model saw this as a significant risk for bar exam success.

Your undergraduate GPA came next in importance and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction modestly toward passing. At 3.10 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the positive effect was limited.

Your first-year law school grades ranked third. Placing in the 8th decile was actually better than the average of 6th decile among accepted students and therefore helped reduce the predicted risk of failure. Unfortunately, this positive contribution was not large enough to offset the impact of your LSAT score.

Taken together, the model concluded your overall profile suggested a slightly higher than even chance of failing the bar. To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as this was the dominant factor in the rejection. Improving that single area would likely shift your predicted probability enough to change the outcome.
